source.title: The Misery of Mechanistic Interpretability: A Formal Perspective

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies the faithfulness and paraphrase robustness of interpretable replacement networks (IRNs), not the claim versions about neuron poles, neuron explanations, or neuron-based circuit analysis. Its results are adjacent findings about IRN feature stability, rather than tests of a listed version.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports the paper's own top-20 active-feature Jaccard results under paraphrase perturbations; these are recorded as findings about feature stability, not as tests of the listed claim versions. The paper's formal-faithfulness results and cited findings do not measure neuron-pole job counts or the listed explanation-scoring outcomes. The underlying-model next-token flip rate is mentioned as context for interpreting the IRN feature-overlap results, not as a test of a listed version.
record.test_reason: The paper measures how stable sparse autoencoder and transcoder feature sets are under paraphrase, and gives formal bounds on how closely these replacement networks match the model. It never audits raw neuron poles (V1, V2, V4), never examines InceptionV1 (V3), never builds neuron-based attribution graphs (V5), and never scores neuron explanations against held-out activations (V6, V7). It only asserts, citing Elhage et al., that MLP neurons are polysemantic. Its replacement-network error results bear on the motivation behind V5 but do not test it.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that existing IRNs are unfaithful under meaning-preserving perturbations across five model families, with formally certified gaps that widen with depth. Verification-aware training narrows the gap (about −90%), but certified feature retention stays low (2–3 of 20). They attribute this partly to the underlying model's own fragility: 21% next-token flips under MINOR paraphrase.
record.recipe_differences: Measures IRN feature-set stability and formal model-to-IRN faithfulness under paraphrase perturbations; it does not use the original neuron-explanation scoring method. The paper combines paraphrase attacks with reachability verification and verification-aware IRN training.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported feature-overlap values vary by model, IRN type (SAE or transcoder), and paraphrase severity (MINOR, MEDIUM, MAJOR).

fits_no_version.finding: Paraphrase attacks sharply cut top-20 active-feature overlap in SAEs and transcoders across five model families. For example, the GPT-2 SAE minimum Jaccard falls to 0.27 (MINOR) and 0.05 (MAJOR). A targeted attack on the Gemma 2 SAE removes all four biological features from the top 8 (Jaccard 0.23).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Replacement-network feature interpretations are not robust to meaning-preserving paraphrases.

fits_no_version.finding: Certified faithfulness gaps between IRNs and the model are substantial at every layer and widen in deeper layers in all five models (Figs. 4, 9, 11, 12). Verification-aware training cuts the GPT-2 layer-6 gap by about 90%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Off-the-shelf replacement networks deviate from the model's computation under small input perturbations, increasingly with depth. This is context for, but not a test of, V5's argument against replacement models.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code and Lean formalizations are released as supplementary material)
record.problems: The reported J values are attack-derived upper bounds from tested perturbations, not worst-case guarantees. The authors note that a single attack cannot rule out lower overlap under another adversarial input. Main-body formal verification results focus mainly on GPT-2; cross-model faithfulness plots are largely figure-based. The paper also acknowledges that its perturbation hulls are too small for full-model compositional verification.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from Table 1's separately reported minimum and mean J values or the Appendix A targeted example. Formal faithfulness-gap figures and training-regime results were not cataloged because they measure model-to-IRN reconstruction bounds rather than any listed claim version or neuron-pole job count.

untested.parts: All: no neuron-pole audit of Qwen3-32B.
All: no neuron job-share measurement in any model.
All: no vision models or canonical polysemantic neuron examples.
All: no measurement of the share of interpretable neurons by architecture or tool.
No neuron-based attribution graphs are built; only replacement-network faithfulness is measured.
No test of activating-example explanations against firing on new text.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Rows correctly carry versions none. The table label 'Qwen 1.5B' is R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B per Table 3. Bills et al. (an original source) is cited only as the auto-interp method; Heap et al. is cited, not measured here. The faithfulness-gap figures are declared in rows_left_out and bear on no version, so they are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job proportions and understood/unknown shares.
Whether those proportions hold across model families, architectures, or scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain interpretability rates, including the InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Whether attribution graphs made from a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a replacement model.
The paper does not test explanations generated from activating examples against new examples to determine where a neuron fires.
The paper does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
